d: Used of the voice
ety: From Stentor + -ian, from Ancient Greek Στέντωρ (Sténtōr). Stentor was the herald of the Greek forces in the Iliad, noted for his loud voice.
s: There seemed no one to dispute his claims when he said, or rather shouted, in stentorian tones: "I am Tsa. This is my she. Who wishes her more than Tsa?"

d: Of or involving dispute or controversy
ety: From polemic + -al. By surface analysis, polem- + -ic + -al.
s: Not only are all these allegations worded in an unnecessarily polemical style, they are also simply false

d: Make dirty or spotty, as by exposure to air; also used metaphorically
ety: First attested during the last quarter of the 15th century, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English maculaten (“to spoil, polute”), borrowed from Latin maculātus, perfect passive participle of maculō (“to spot”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).
s: There was a fresh smell in the air. Sidewalks began to be maculated with spreading areas of dryness

d: A specially long, formal letter
ety: The noun is derived from Middle English epistel, epistole, pistel (“letter; literary work in letter form; written legend or story; spoken communication; (Christianity) one of the letters by an apostle in the New Testament; extract from such a letter read as part of the Mass”) [and other forms], and then partly: * from Old English epistol, epistola, pistol (“letter, epistle”), from Latin epistola (
s: Wide flew the doors, and lo, / Messire de Beringhen, and this epistle!

d: Any formal system of reasoning that arrives at the truth by the exchange of logical arguments
ety: From Old French dialectique, from Late Latin dialectica, from Ancient Greek διαλεκτική (dialektikḗ, “the art of argument through interactive questioning and answering”), from διαλεκτικός (dialektikós, “relating to dialogue”), from διαλέγομαι (dialégomai, “to participate in a dialogue”), from διά (diá, “through, across”) + λέγειν (légein, “to speak”).
s: This situation created the inner dialectic of American history.

d: A woman’s drawstring handbag; usually made of net or beading or brocade; used in 18th and 19th centuries
ety: From French réticule, from Latin rēticulum, diminutive of rēte (“net”). Doublet of reticle, reticulum, and Reticulum.
s: Eleanor wore a green silk dress to bring out here eyes, with an ivory tatted collar and reticule to match.

d: A form of life insurance whereby on the death or default of a participant his share is distributed to the remaining members
ety: From French tontine, named after Lorenzo de Tonti, who introduced the scheme into France in around 1653. Thus, from Tonti + -ine.
s: They were pleasantly high, but in an almost self-conscious way, as if they were members of a tontine blessed by the unexpected death of two or three of its members.

d: Frenzied as if possessed by a demon
ety: From Latin daemoniacus + -al.
s: The spectator feels almost persuaded that he is witnessing some unearthly demoniacal orgie.

d: Bring to a desired consistency, texture, or hardness by a process of gradually heating and cooling
ety: From Middle English anelen, onelen, from Old English onǣlan (“to burn, ignite, set fire to, consume, heat, enlighten, incite, inflame, inspire, kindle”), from Proto-Germanic *ana (“on”) + Proto-Germanic *ailijaną (“to burn”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eydʰ- (“to burn”). The double-N spelling may have arisen by analogy with Latinate verbs like announce, annex, and annul. The word is related to Ol
s: The experience annealed them, strengthening their resolve.

d: Cry loudly, as of animals
ety: From Middle English ȝameren, ȝaumeren, yemeren, ȝomeren, from Old English ġeōmrian (“to lament”), from Proto-West Germanic *jāmarōn, from Proto-Germanic *jēmarōną (“to show misery or sadness”), from Proto-Germanic *jēmaraz (“miserable, sorrowful, sad”), from Proto-Indo-European *yem- (“to hold, match, defeat”). Reinforced by cognate Middle Dutch jammeren (modern Dutch jammeren), from the same ulti
s: It was a ship, but a whale to the Dark Nebula’s minnow; and on its side was the Spaceship-and-Sun of the Empire. Every alarm on the ship yammered hysterically.

d: Identifying word or words by which someone or something is called and classified or distinguished from others
ety: From late Middle English appellacion, from Old French apellatiun, from Latin appellātiō (“a naming”).
s: Russian River flows through a country of hill ridges, which in many places are dignifiable with the appellation of mountains.

d: Divide into two or more branches so as to form a fork
ety: From Medieval Latin furcātus (“forked, branched”), from Latin furca (“fork”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Compare French fourchu. The verb was formed by metanalysis or as if from Latin furcō (“to fork”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).
s: Descending keel of the pronotum, which divides into two furcating lamella

d: A system of clandestine printing and distribution of dissident or banned literature
ety: Borrowed from Russian самизда́т (samizdát, “self-publishing”), from сам (sam, “self”) + изда́т (izdát), an abbreviation of изда́тельство (izdátelʹstvo, “publishing house, publishing”) (compare Russian Госизда́т (Gosizdát, “State Publisher”)).
s: This was the first time she was reading it, for she'd never managed to get a samizdat copy in Moscow.

d: (especially of certain salts) becoming liquid by absorbing moisture from the air
ety: Latin deliquescens, present participle of deliquesco; de + liquesco (“to melt”): compare French déliquescent. By surface analysis, deliquesce + -ent
s: “Any one who stands outside, who hides himself in a deliquescent aloofness, is a sneak and a spy—”

d: A favorable omen
ety: From Middle French auspice, from Latin auspicium, in turn from auspex.
s: The circle of vultures was not a good auspice.

d: Lacking taste or flavor or tang
ety: From French insipide, from Latin īnsipidus (“tasteless”), from in- (“not”) + sapidus (“savory”). In some senses, perhaps influenced by insipient (“unwise, foolish, stupid”).
s: The textbook had a most insipid presentation of the controversy.

d: Disagreeable aftereffects from the use of drugs (especially alcohol)
ety: Borrowed from German Katzenjammer (“hangover”, literally “the wailing of cats”); a determinative compound formed from Katze (“cat”) + -n- + Jammer (“wailing; lamentation”).
s: Also, I had found my way into the realm of the mind, and I was intellectually intoxicated. (Alas! as I was to learn at a later period, intellectual intoxication too, has its katzenjammer.)

d: An inn in some eastern countries with a large courtyard that provides accommodation for caravans
ety: Borrowed either: * from Middle French carvansera, carvassera (modern French caravansérail, carauanserrail (obsolete), caravansara (obsolete)); or * directly from its etymon Ottoman Turkish كاروانسَرای (karvanseray), كَروانسَرای (kervanseray) (modern Turkish kervansaray), from Old Anatolian Turkish [script needed] (kārvān-serā); or * directly from its etymon Persian کاروانسرای (kârvânsarây), from ک
s: Think, in this batter'd Caravanserai / Whose Doorways are alternate Night and Day, / How Sultán after Sultán with his Pomp / Abode his Hour or two, and went his way.

d: A piece of cloth sewn under an opening
ety: Either a variant of placard or borrowed from Middle French plaquette (“metal plate”), from plaquer (“to lay or clap on”). See placard.
s: Dislike dressing together. Nicked myself shaving. Biting her nether lip, hooking the placket of her skirt.

d: Informal terms for money
ety: From Dutch boedel. Doublet of bottle (dialectal term meaning building or house).
s: He was your 'man higher up' when you were on the force. His share of the boodle passed through your hands. You must go on the stand and testify against him.

d: A situation from which extrication is difficult especially an unpleasant or trying one
ety: 16th century. Origin unknown; perhaps a dialectal corruption (simulating a word of Latin origin with suffix -ary) of wandreth (“evil, plight, peril, adversity, difficulty”), from Middle English wandreth, from Old Norse vandræði (“difficulty, trouble”), from vándr (“difficult, requiring pains and care”).
s: What a difficult quandary for a bright, talented child!

d: Make saw-toothed or jag the edge of
ety: Borrowed from Latin serrātus, past participle of serrō.
s: Serrate the edges of the teeth.

d: The system of patronage in communist countries; controlled by committees in the Communist Party
ety: Borrowed from Russian номенклату́ра (nomenklatúra), from Latin nōmenclātūra (“a calling by name, list of names”), from nomen (“name”) + calare (“call”). Doublet of nomenclature.
s: During the long rule of Leonid Brezhnev (1964–1982), the nomenklatura had cemented their power in the system.

d: A variation in circumstances or fortune at different times in your life or in the development of something
ety: From Middle French vicissitude, from Latin vicissitūdō (“change”), from vicissim (“on the other hand, in turn”), from vicis (“change, vicissitude”), whence Portuguese vez and French fois (“time (as in "next time"), occurrence”).
s: And God made.. the Stars, and set them in the firmament of Heaven to illuminate the Earth, and rule the day in their vicissitude...

d: Having the sticky properties of an adhesive
ety: From Late Latin viscidus, from viscum (“birdlime”).
s: The pool’s bottoms and sides were lined with a blanket of viscid slime, and the three statues in the middle, the three Sirens of Titan, were under a mucilaginous hump.

d: Hairdressing consisting of a perfumed oil or ointment
ety: From French pommade, from Italian pomata (“ointment, pomade”), from pomo (“apple”) + -ata (“-ade, -ate: forming nouns”), from Latin pōmum (“fruit, apple”). Doublet of pomatum, pomate, and pomace. Early pomades tended to be various kinds of fat mixed with apples for a more pleasing scent.
s: The rain beat my hair, run down my face and into my mouth so that I can taste the coconut oil pomade from my hair.

d: A term of address for an English lord
ety: From French milord, from English my Lord. Compare milady.
s: Not since the year 17—, when milord Castlebrilliant's curricle was whirled to sea with her ladyship within, had there been such vehement weather.

d: Ask for or request earnestly
ety: From Late Middle English adjuren (“to bind (oneself or someone) by oath to do something; to entreat or implore (someone); to question (someone) under oath”), from Anglo-Norman adjurer, Middle French adjurer, and Old French ajurer (“to bind (oneself or someone) under oath; to entreat or implore (someone)”) (modern French adjurer), and from their etymon Latin adiūrāre, the present active infinitive
s: Party members are adjured to promote awareness of this problem.

d: Dark and gloomy
ety: ] From Middle English tenebrose, from Anglo-Norman tenebrous (earlier tenebrus), from Latin tenebrōsus, itself from tenebrae (“darkness, shadows”).
s: White was more delicate, more feminine, more beautiful. Dark was more robust, more masculine, more tenebrous.

d: One bound by vows to a religion or life of worship or service
ety: From Latin votus, past participle of vovere (“to vow, to devote”).
s: Well then, ye who delight in laughter, ye who are votaries of the proverb, "Laugh and grow Fat;"

d: Encourage or assent to illegally or criminally
ety: From French conniver (“to ignore and thus become complicit in wrongdoing”), or directly from its etymon Latin con(n)īvēre (“close or screw up the eyes, blink, wink; overlook, turn a blind eye, connive”) (perhaps alluding to two persons involved in a scheme together winking to each other), from con- (prefix indicating a being or bringing together of several objects) + *nīvēre (related to nictō (“to
s: Out of reverence to Cato, he for a while connived her impurity and immodesty, but at length dismissed her.

d: Large open car seating four with folding top
ety: Borrowed from French phaéton.
s: ...I saw the girls of Nob Hill on their way to school, kicking pebbles at each other and laughing; I saw young ladies coming home past curfew in their beaus' phaetons...

d: Marked by refinement in taste and manners
ety: Borrowed from French gentil (“gentile”), from Latin gentīlis (“of or belonging to the same people or nation”), from gēns (“clan; tribe; people, family”) + adjective suffix -īlis (“-ile”). Doublet of gentle, gentile, and jaunty. See also gens, gender, genus, and generation.
s: Genteel America was handicapped by meagerness of soul, thinness of temper, paucity of talent.

d: Pretentious or silly talk or writing
ety: Phonetic spelling of bologna.
s: That's a bunch of baloney! I don't believe one word!

d: Easily irritated or annoyed
ety: From Middle French, from Latin petulāns, akin to petō (“to ask for”).
s: Lack of sleep is causing Dave's recent petulant behavior.

d: A severe recurring vascular headache; occurs more frequently in women than men
ety: Borrowed from Middle French migraigne, semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin hēmicrānia (“pain in one half of the head”), from Ancient Greek ἡμικρᾱνίᾰ (hēmikrāníă), from ἡμι- (hēmi-, “hemi-, half”) + κρανίον (kraníon, “skull”) (whence also English cranium). Doublet of migraine and hemicrania.
s: For quotations using this term, see Citations:megrim.

d: Run away; usually includes taking something or somebody along
s: The thieves absconded with our property.

d: Medication that prevents the formation of gas in the alimentary tract or eases its passing
ety: From Latin carminātus (“carded”), past participle of Latin carminō (“to card, produce by carding; hence to cleanse”), from carmen (“a card for freeing wool or flax from the coarser parts, and from extraneous matter”).
s: “A mental carminative,” said Mr. Scogan reflectively. “That's what you need.”

d: A Buddhist and Hindu and especially Jainist doctrine holding that all forms of life are sacred and urging the avoidance of violence
ety: Borrowed from Sanskrit अहिंसा (ahiṃsā).
s: This, in essence, is the Jain doctrine of ahimsa – a direct inversion of Vedic beliefs about the sustaining powers of animal sacrifice.

d: Marked by qualities giving the power to produce an intended effect
ety: From Old French efficacieux (whence -acious), from Latin efficāx (“efficacious”) + -ous, from efficere (“to effect, to accomplish”); see effect.
s: He would weep for hours together, and I verily believe that to the very end this spoilt child of life thought his weak tears in some way efficacious.
